summary: Brick light and fog-signal building at the lake end of Duluth's ship-canal breakwater, lit in 1901 to replace an 1874 wooden light; the city has argued over its foghorn since the 1890s.

lens.where: Lake Superior Maritime Visitor Center, Canal Park (the active light is now an LED beacon)

access.note: Building not open to the public; owned by the Lake Superior Marine Museum Association since 2025, with the Coast Guard operating the light and fog signal; tours hoped for 2027. Seen from the canal piers.

facts.agency: Lake Superior Marine Museum Association (owner since 2025); U.S. Coast Guard operates the light and fog signal

events.note: Congress appropriates $10,000 for a light at the canal entrance (Pepper: March 1870); LighthouseFriends says the Light-House Board asked for $10,000 in 1870 after six petitions

A violent storm tears a large part of the wooden south breakwater apart while the contractors are building the dwelling and elevated walk; work stops for the season (LighthouseFriends: the south pier was damaged by a storm the previous fall; temporary light on the north pier by May 1873)
Wooden pyramidal tower at the offshore end of the south breakwater, with frame keeper's dwelling and elevated walkway
Operational 2 June 1874: fifth-order Fresnel lens, fixed red, focal plane 40 ft, 12.5 miles

Fourth-order Fresnel lens by Barbier and Fenestre (nomination; LighthouseFriends dates the change to a fixed red fourth-order light to 1886; Pepper gives 1877 as the lens's manufacture and the upgrade date as unidentified)
Automated fog bell (nomination); LighthouseFriends dates it 1879 and says it came from South Manitou Island
Wooden fog-signal building with a pair of steam-powered whistles; first assistant keeper added

Disputed: LighthouseFriends says the 1885 red-and-white flashing light became a fixed red light of the fourth order in 1886 (the nomination has the fourth-order lens from 1877 and mentions no flashing period)
Inner (rear) Light established, making a range; the 1874 light renamed the South Breakwater Outer Light; Congress had appropriated $3,284.12 on 2 March 1889
Parabolic reflector built over one of the steam whistles to deaden the sound toward Duluth; whistles ran some 1,048 hours that year
Wooden Inner and Outer Lights demolished and temporary lights used while the concrete south breakwater is finished (light and fog signal moved to temporary structures 1 November 1900)
Brick combined light tower and fog-signal building on a concrete pier on a timber crib, by the Eleventh Lighthouse District
Present building first lit 1 September 1901 with the 1877 fourth-order lens
Brick duplex for the two assistant keepers finished in February 1913 (they had rented housing in the city since 1901)
Steam fog whistles replaced by a pair of steam locomotive whistles
Type F diaphone worked by compressed air replaces the locomotive whistles (October 1923, Pepper); Duluth residents complain and a sound deflector is added
Diaphone replaced by an electric fog signal
Nomination: resident keepers until 1976 (Duluth Preservation Alliance gives 1970)
Diaphones from Kewaunee, Wisconsin, reactivated by TOOT on 1 April 1995
Fourth-order Fresnel lens (in service since 1877) retired and replaced by an LED beacon
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places (reference 16000341)
Declared excess by the Coast Guard and offered under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act
Ownership passes to the Lake Superior Marine Museum Association; sale closed March 2025; Coast Guard keeps the right to maintain its aids to navigation

wrecks.outcome: Whaleback freighter sank about a mile from the Duluth Harbor Ship Canal after a collision; the nomination lists her among vessels in the light's vicinity, and no source read ties a rescue or a keeper's action to this light

evidence.supports: light and fog signal in one white brick building with a red roof; tower; pier
evidence.quote: The superstructure consists of a one-and-a-half story rectangular fog signal building with an integral two-story light tower surmounted by a lantern.

evidence.supports: white with a red roof
evidence.quote: The Duluth Harbor South Breakwater Outer Light is painted white and has a red roof.

evidence.supports: about 1,000 feet from shore at the east end of the south breakwater
evidence.quote: This property is situated approximately 1,000 feet from shore at the eastern end of the Ship Canal's southern breakwater.

evidence.supports: range with the Inner Light
evidence.quote: Mariners navigate their vessels to align the taller Inner Light directly above the shorter Outer Light in order to follow the proper course for safe entry.

evidence.supports: operational 2 June 1874
evidence.quote: The Duluth South Breakwater Light became operational on 2 June 1874.

evidence.supports: present building operational 1 September 1901
evidence.quote: The South Breakwater Outer Light became operational on 1 September 1901.

evidence.supports: Minnesota Point is the northern strand of the longest freshwater sand spit; 7 miles; Superior Entry
evidence.quote: The world's longest freshwater sand spit is located at Lake Superior's southwestern end. Its northern strand, named Minnesota Point, extends some seven miles southward from adjoining uplands to what was a natural channel where the St. Louis River emptied into the lake. This channel came to be called the Superior Entry.

evidence.supports: Minnesota and Wisconsin Points separate the lake from the harbor
evidence.quote: Minnesota Point and Wisconsin Point separate Lake Superior from a large natural harbor consisting of the waters of Allouez Bay and the lower St. Louis River.

evidence.supports: competition with Superior prompted the canal
evidence.quote: Economic competition between the two ports provided an impetus in 1870 for business interests favoring Duluth to undertake excavation of a canal across Minnesota Point.

evidence.supports: canal opened April 1871
evidence.quote: This led to the opening of the Duluth Harbor Ship Canal in April 1871.

evidence.supports: canal width and length
evidence.quote: The Duluth Harbor Ship Canal is 300 feet wide and approximately 0.3 mile long including its north pier and south breakwater.

evidence.supports: Minnesota Point Lighthouse, first federal lighthouse near Duluth, 1858-1885, marked the Superior Entry
evidence.quote: Now in ruins, it was the first Federal lighthouse constructed in the Duluth vicinity and operated from 1858 to 1885. The Minnesota Point Lighthouse marked the Superior Entry inlet

evidence.supports: Minnesota Point Lighthouse six miles southeast
evidence.quote: Another historic property is the Minnesota Point Lighthouse, located approximately six miles southeast from the Duluth Harbor South Breakwater Outer Light.

evidence.supports: Board asked Congress for $10,000 in 1870 after six petitions
evidence.quote: The Lighthouse Board asked Congress for $10,000 in 1870 to build a lighthouse at Duluth, after having received six petitions for its construction.

evidence.supports: petitioners: easy by day, difficult and dangerous at night in thick weather
evidence.quote: difficult and dangerous at night when the weather is thick

evidence.supports: fog makes the canal entrance hard to see
evidence.quote: Foggy conditions on western Lake Superior sometimes makes it difficult for approaching vessels to discern the Duluth Harbor Ship Canal's narrow entrance.

evidence.supports: Congress appropriated $10,000 in March 1870
evidence.quote: Congress appropriated $10,000 for the construction of a light at the canal's entrance in March 1870.

evidence.supports: site was the outer end of the south breakwater; construction waited until 1872
evidence.quote: Deciding that the best location for the new light would be on the outer end of the new south breakwater, construction had to wait until 1872 when the new breakwater was planned for completion.

evidence.supports: work began late in the summer of 1872
evidence.quote: work began late in the summer of that year.

evidence.supports: dwelling built on shore, then storm tore the breakwater apart and work stopped
evidence.quote: After the construction of a keepers dwelling on shore at the inner end of the pier, the crew had turned their attention to the construction of the elevated walk when a violent storm ripped a large part of the wooden breakwater apart, forcing work to be abandoned for the season.

evidence.supports: by May 1873 seven-room dwelling and part of the walkway done; temporary light on the north pier
evidence.quote: By May 1873, a seven-room keeper's dwelling and a portion of an elevated walkway were completed

evidence.supports: temporary light on north pier until south pier repaired
evidence.quote: a temporary light was placed on the outer end of the north pier and work was suspended until the south pier could be repaired.

evidence.supports: wooden pyramidal tower, dwelling and elevated walkway
evidence.quote: The canal's need for a lighted aid to navigation led the U.S. Lighthouse Establishment to construct a wooden pyramidal tower lighthouse at the south breakwater's offshore end.

evidence.supports: dwelling and elevated walkway for inclement weather
evidence.quote: A wood-framed keeper's dwelling was also built nearby, and a wooden elevated walkway was erected along the south breakwater between the lighthouse and shore to allow for access during inclement weather.

evidence.supports: general: pier end marked by small fourth- or fifth-order light on a frame tower
evidence.quote: The end of one pier is marked by a small light of the fourth or fifth order, supported on a frame structure either square or polygonal.

evidence.supports: general: towers could be moved out when the pier was extended
evidence.quote: When the pier is extended these towers can be readily moved out to the end.

evidence.supports: finished January 1874, commissioned 2 June 1874
evidence.quote: was finished in January 1874 and commissioned on June 2, 1874.

evidence.supports: fifth-order Fresnel, fixed red, 40 ft, 12.5 miles
evidence.quote: Its optic was a fifth order Fresnel lens that signaled a fixed red light with a focal plane 40 feet above water level. It could be seen for 12.5 miles in clear weather.

evidence.supports: 1877 fourth-order lens by Barbier and Fenestre
evidence.quote: This optic was replaced in 1877 with a more powerful fourth order Fresnel lens manufactured by Barbier and Fenestre of Paris, France.

evidence.supports: 1885 red-and-white flashes; 1886 fixed red fourth-order
evidence.quote: The characteristic of the light was changed from fixed red to alternate red and white flashes spaced by ten seconds at the opening of navigation in 1885, but in 1886, the fifth-order, flashing red and white light was changed to a fixed red light of the fourth order.

evidence.supports: date of the lens upgrade unidentified; lens made 1877
evidence.quote: at an as yet unidentified date, the Fifth Order lens was upgraded to a fixed red Fourth Order Fresnel lens manufactured by Barbier & Fenestre of Paris in 1877.

evidence.supports: fourth-order lens in service since 1877 retired 2014
evidence.quote: In 2014 the Coast Guard determined that the fourth order Fresnel lens that had been in service since 1877 needed to be retired.

evidence.supports: fog bell 1880; 1885 fog-signal building with steam whistles
evidence.quote: an automated fog bell was installed at the South Breakwater Light in 1880. This bell was replaced in 1885 when a wooden fog signal building was built on the south breakwater near the lighthouse and equipped with a pair of steam-powered fog whistles.

evidence.supports: bell dated 1879, previously used on South Manitou Island
evidence.quote: In 1879, a fog bell, previously used on South Manitou Island, was mounted in a house near the tower and was struck by machinery when needed.

evidence.supports: appropriation for range lights at Duluth Harbor
evidence.quote: Duluth Harbor, Minnesota: For establishing range-lights at Duluth Harbor, three thousand two hundred and eighty-four dollars and twelve cents.

evidence.supports: act approved 2 March 1889
evidence.quote: Approved, March 2, 1889.

evidence.supports: 1889 Inner Light; older light renamed Outer
evidence.quote: A range light system was established at the Ship Canal in 1889 when the Duluth Harbor South Breakwater Inner Light became operational. It was a wooden pyramidal tower that was taller than the 1874 breakwater light, which was renamed the South Breakwater Outer Light.

evidence.supports: ships align the taller light above the shorter
evidence.quote: Mariners navigate their vessels to align the taller Inner Light directly above the shorter Outer Light in order to follow the proper course for safe entry.

evidence.supports: the Board's reports call the station Duluth (front range)
evidence.quote: Duluth (front range), Minnesota. — This 10-inch steam whistle was in operation some 334 hours, consuming about 21 tons of coal.

evidence.supports: the nomination's source list includes a 1910 description of Duluth Range Front Light Station
evidence.quote: Description of buildings, premises, equipment, etc., at Duluth Range Front Light Station, Minnesota, September 6, 1910.

evidence.supports: 1895 appropriation of three million dollars
evidence.quote: In 1895 the U.S . Congress appropriated three million dollars to improve the ports of Duluth and Superior.

evidence.supports: Pepper dates the appropriation to 1896
evidence.quote: Congress combined the Duluth and Superior ports into one entity in 1896 and appropriated three million dollars for the Army Corps of Engineers

evidence.supports: concrete breakwater and pier finished 1900; wooden lights replaced with temporary lights
evidence.quote: The Ship Canal gained a concrete south breakwater and concrete north pier which were completed in 1900. During the course of this work the south breakwater's wooden Inner and Outer Lights were demolished and replaced with temporary lights.

evidence.supports: drawings for a combined light tower and fog-signal building
evidence.quote: Drawings of a combined light tower and fog signal building

evidence.supports: light and fog signal moved to temporary structures 1 Nov 1900
evidence.quote: signal moved to temporarv structures November 1, 1900.

evidence.supports: temporary structure and fog-signal plant; 25-ft tower and 37-ft mast
evidence.quote: one of the fog-signal plants was transferred from the old pier and installed therein. A pyramidal tower 25 feet high was erected at the outer end of the pier and a mast 37 feet long was set up at the inner end.

evidence.supports: 700-foot elevated walk moved to the new pier
evidence.quote: The old elevated walk, 700 feet long, was removed from the old pier and was repaired and erected on the new pier.

evidence.supports: Eleventh District built replacement, operational 1 Sept 1901 with 1877 lens and 1885 whistles
evidence.quote: The Eleventh U.S. Lighthouse District, which had jurisdiction over Duluth, undertook the construction of replacement lighthouses and completed work on the south breakwater's new Inner and Outer Lights in 1901.

evidence.supports: equipped with the 1877 lens and 1885 whistles and steam plant
evidence.quote: equipped with the 1877 fourth order Fresnel lens and 1885 fog whistles and steam plant.

evidence.supports: 1877 lens had been in the original 1874 lighthouse
evidence.quote: The original beacon light installed in 1901 was a fourth order Fresnel lens manufactured in 1877 by Barbier and Fenestre of Paris. It had been previously installed in the original Duluth Harbor South Breakwater Lighthouse

evidence.supports: concrete pier on timber crib filled with rock; 21 ft water
evidence.quote: The lighthouse's foundation is a rectangular pier built of concrete that is supported by a massive timber crib filled with rock. It sits upon submerged land at the south breakwater's offshore (eastern) end where the water depth is 21 feet.

evidence.supports: pier 100 by 36 ft, rises about 18 ft
evidence.quote: This foundation is approximately 100 feet long east-west by 36 feet wide north-south.

evidence.supports: pier rises about 18 ft
evidence.quote: and rises to approximately 18 feet above water level.

evidence.supports: Cream City brick on a stone base
evidence.quote: This part of the structure includes a three-foot tall base made with cut stone that supports brick masonry exterior walls. The fabric above the stone base is buff-colored, machine-made Cream City brick.

evidence.supports: fog signal building 45 by 20 ft
evidence.quote: It is 45 feet long east-west by 20 feet wide

evidence.supports: tower 35 ft tall, 8 ft on a side, in the southeast corner
evidence.quote: It is 35 feet tall, rectangular in plan, and measures eight feet long on each side.

evidence.supports: cast-iron spiral stair
evidence.quote: a cast iron spiral stairway leads upward two stories to an overhead metal trapdoor

evidence.supports: basement with tunnel to shore for sheltered movement in bad weather
evidence.quote: The basement's southern end includes an opening to a tunnel extending to shore beneath the south breakwater's deck. This tunnel provided for sheltered movement between shore and the lighthouse during times of inclement weather.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record lists a tower built 1874 as standing and a 'Tower 2' of 1901. The 1874 wooden pyramidal tower was pulled down in 1900 when the concrete south breakwater was built; the standing brick building is the 1901 one.

notes_for_editor: 1) ROSTER IDENTITY: the USLHS archive has no roster under 'Duluth South Breakwater Range Front (Outer)' (0 lines). The keepers sit under its place 'Duluth Harbor North Breakwater' (est. 1910, roster 1873-1970), which is the shared roster of the Duluth canal lights; LighthouseFriends prints the same names for this Outer Light, with differences: it omits Arthur J. Cater (first assistant 1916), gives John Woods as 1934-at least 1940 where the archive gives 1934-1940, and lists no laborer. The same men also served the Inner Light (and the North Pier Light from 1910), so the roster is the canal station's, not the Outer Light alone. The Woods identification (second assistant 1898-1902, Grand Marais, Superior Entry, Duluth 1934-1940) rests on the USLHS person record linking them. 2) CONFLICTS stated in the story: lens (nomination 1877; LighthouseFriends 1886 fixed red fourth-order after 1885 flashes; Pepper: upgrade date unidentified); fog bell (1880 nomination, 1879 LighthouseFriends); harbor appropriation (1895 nomination, 1896 Pepper); automation (1976 nomination and Destination Duluth, 1970 Duluth Preservation Alliance); head keeper's house built 1873 (LighthouseFriends, DPA) or 1874 (nomination, Pepper); range 17 miles (nomination, Seaway Review) vs 13 nautical miles after the LED (LighthouseFriends); Wikipedia gives the diaphones as 1921 but the nomination and Pepper say 1923 (Wikipedia not cited). 3) The Commissioner of Lighthouses 1915 table prints 'Duluth Range Front, Mich.' (state misprinted); read as this light because it is the only Duluth front range. 4) NEWSPAPERS: three Chronicling America searches (MN papers, 1888-1925, keeper and fog-whistle terms) found nothing about this light; Duluth dailies are not in the Library's collection. LHB reports before 1891 are not in the corpus, so the 1870s-80s chronology rests on the nomination, LighthouseFriends and Pepper; the 1870 petition quotation comes through LighthouseFriends. 5) No women keepers or family members who kept the light appear in the sources read. No rescue or wreck is tied to this light by a source read (the Thomas A. Wilson is listed only as a nearby vessel). 6) 1960s-70 roster lines are Coast Guard personnel named exactly as the archive prints them, with no personal details. 7) Structure types use the closest DESIGN vocabulary (the brick tower is square, not conical; filed as conical_masonry 'brick or stone tower'). The 1873/74 head keeper's house is listed as a standing structure on the nomination's word (it says both dwellings remain standing); the Duluth Preservation Alliance gives its address (private status not checked, so the story gives no house numbers). 8) FACT-CHECK 2026-10-21 (independent pass; all 26 sources re-read or checked against the cached text): (a) LighthouseFriends calls Bishop the longest-serving head keeper, but the register gives Prior 20 years and Bishop 15; the story now says so. (b) The nomination's 100 by 36 ft pier is today's: the same nomination says the original pier was narrower and was strengthened in the late twentieth century; the story no longer presents it as the 1901 size. (c) The nomination gives the main block as 45 by 20 ft; Pepper gives 22 ft wide (and the 1901 description LighthouseFriends reprints says 22 by 45 ft); both are now stated. (d) LighthouseFriends' list is not identical to the archive's: it omits Arthur J. Cater (first assistant 1916) and orders Reynolds/Nichol and Watt/Sullivan the other way round; the story says 'almost the same list'. (e) The Duluth Preservation Alliance citation is the blog's rolling index page, which held the 'Duluth Canal & Lightkeepers' Residences' entry when read; no permalink was found by search. (f) The story quotes two short fragments that LighthouseFriends reprints from older primary texts (the 1870 petition and Bishop's 1937 interview); the editor may trim one if the one-quotation rule for LighthouseFriends is applied strictly. (g) The nomination gives 12.5 and 17 'miles' without saying statute or nautical; the story says so. (h) The 1915 Commissioner table prints the state of 'Duluth Range Front' as Michigan; it sits in the Eleventh District column list with Marquette and Fort Gratiot, so it is read as this light. (i) Coast Guard names (48 in the archive's USCG block, 1960-1970, plus 8 principal keepers of those years) appear only in the roster as the archive prints them, with no personal details; none is named in the prose. (j) The story's Thomas A. Wilson sentence only restates the nomination's list of nearby National Register vessels; the nomination does not tie that wreck to this light.
